items.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020
items.q: I think I would probably throw Metheny and Stan Getz in there

ctx.x: How does it matter in my eyes? Well that’s too big a question to answer, God, how do you even begin? See since I was very young I loved black music. There were — radio was entirely segregated. There were white stations and black stations. The black ones were KDIA and KSOL. And I started listening to that. It was a revelation. It wasn’t something that most people in my circle would have ever listened to. I was asked to join a sort of rainbow soul band with — to be the saxophonist in a group that was Korean,…

role. This is functional music, this is culture, this is social interrelationships. And to see that was just an eye opening experience for an 18-year-old kid who grew up in Jewish culture you know. It was fantastic. And I think there are many other anecdotal instant answers like that of just experiencing life in ways in which musics of African-American origin had a cultural meaning that I didn’t find elsewhere. It wasn’t a split between music and life. I think another component of the answer that can go down a…

Okay. Well the more we talk the more I think we have in common, because I had a similar experience in growing up in Rochester with the kind of thing you’re describing so I thank you for sharing that with me. You used the word “functional.” And over my shoulder I have Count Basie and Lester Young and I think of them as playing, I guess, functional music. I mean people could dance to it, they took joy in it, it hit their solar plexuses perhaps more than their head. I’m not sure that’s the way to put it but, so I’m…
